name: Tomas Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day at the firm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The restaurant clients tend to arrive with a bag of receipts just before lunch. I sort the accounts, check tax returns against the invoices, and call when a number does not add up. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification; after years doing this I know the work fairly well, but the rush before filing still wears me down. I enjoy finding the missing receipt that finally makes a restaurant’s accounts explainable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI at work now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Saba works at a building-supply counter, and our school-age children Anya and Yusuf split the kitchen table for homework. We have a mortgage, I earn typical pay for this work, and we have about four months of expenses saved with some other accounting firms nearby. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer the ledger I can explain and a colleague beside me when a process changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The restaurant owners would still bring their invoices in a bag on Thursday. A small sorter would only clear some of the copying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office I am happy for a tool to group receipts if we can trace every amount. I would still want the person signing the return to have seen the actual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my work and normal pay to hold in this picture. We have about four months of expenses saved and some other firms nearby, so the mortgage feels manageable even if one month is untidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking restaurant accounts against the paper invoices and prepare the same year-end returns. I would transfer a fixed forty from each monthly wage into our reserve until it reaches six months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our pay here. My biggest nuisance would still be the last-minute box of crumpled receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the sorter yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and would ask a trained colleague to show me where a total came from before I rely on it. Watching a checked example is enough for now; I would keep my ledger method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why grow the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Saba and I want six months behind us before our older child starts secondary school trips. Forty a month from pay is modest, but it is fresh savings.

I would keep **human sign-off** tied to the original bills.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and normal pay make the mortgage manageable.
The firm still needs my **year-end checks** even with a small sorter.
do: Keep checking **restaurant invoices** and preparing year-end returns.
Transfer **forty monthly** from salary until six months are saved.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software drafts returns and checks totals, the firm may decide it needs fewer middle desks. I would want to hear the plan before the rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers to ask management for the error list and a written policy on whose name goes on a return. I would bring that request through our staff association, with a proposed notice period for reduced hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own review hours could be cut when tax preparation fees fall. Saba works at a building-supply counter, but one wage would not comfortably carry our mortgage and two children for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would meet the staff association delegate next week with the last quarter’s staffing and error figures. If the firm offers a paid, supervised course on its approved tool, I would take it; if my hours fall in the first year, I would apply only to posted accountant jobs whose written pay, hours, and start date cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing paid hours, though four months saved gives me time to insist on written terms. I am not eager to learn a system from an advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm will not fund the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing the present review work and use the professional body’s free written examples at home. I would not try AI on a live client file without a supervisor beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before a new contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vacancy is only a possible job. I would wait for a signed offer with the wage and start date before I give notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would put the next tax seasons under a clock. Robots around 2031 would not postpone what happens to our desks in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm must tell clients who answers for a return when AGI prepares it in 2028. I would ask the staff association to secure severance and notice terms before anyone is told to clear a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my review post or most of its wage to go, even after years in the job. Four months of savings is a real buffer, but the mortgage would consume it fast if Saba’s counter wage were our only income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would cancel the family’s planned long trip and transfer its monthly budget into a cash job-loss account, while joining the association’s severance meeting. If I lose my accounting post in the first year after 2028, I would apply to posted small-business tax liaison jobs only with written mortgage-covering pay, hours, and a start date; I would keep the current wage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large pay loss, not merely a longer day. I can plan with the union, but I cannot create a posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a liaison job be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I doubt any desk job is guaranteed safe after 2028. I would take a paid opening as a bridge while I see what clients still value, not bet the house on a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Anya and Yusuf that the trip is postponed while we protect the house. We would keep their weekly swim lesson until a wage actually stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me learn the difficult client conversations before the routine pages disappear. It would not make an empty vacancy pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues to use the five years before 2031 to negotiate paid client practice and notice before job cuts. AGI hits our account screens then; robots around 2034 matter later to hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think the old review post might shrink, but I could grow a record of explaining tax notices while keeping my salary. Four months of savings gives me a little time to choose a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take one paid client-notice case each quarter only if my manager Oona assigns it and sit with her for the final call. I would transfer forty from each monthly wage into cash; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted client service post only if signed pay, hours, and start date cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual cut, but five years would let me see whether the client work has a budget. I would not leave the current wage for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use the professional body’s free case notes while I keep reviewing returns for pay. If Oona cannot give me paid client time, I would keep those files and wait for an actual opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Saba need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Saba would want the start date and wage written down before we change the household budget. I would show her a signed offer, not my hopes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put both children closer to leaving home. I could still lose the review work, but the next few budgets are not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm has time to keep real apprenticeships before AGI reaches accounts in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not add time to the desk work we do here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect preparation fees to decline eventually, yet our current pay and four-month reserve should hold for the next few years. I would like to reach a six-month buffer and know whether clients still pay for a person to explain their tax notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the current restaurant returns and transfer forty a month from salary until our reserve covers six months. I would practise paid client calls with Oona supervising only if she assigns them; if my review post contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted client service role only with signed wages, hours, and start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about where the profession goes, but not at risk of missing next month’s payment. Ten years is enough to build a track record without quitting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you finally try AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a colleague test a proven tool, but I would not put client data into it on my own without a paid supervised session. I have not used AI yet and am not promising I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anya and Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Anya and Yusuf that I am learning to explain the numbers, not just enter them. I would not call any certificate a job offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut my review post before a paid client service job opens. Written notice, severance agreed in advance, and paid time on real client notices would help. A job move would still need a signed wage and start date that cover the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who will explain a disputed tax bill to a restaurant owner after an automated return goes out. A ledger can be perfect and still leave a frightened person at the counter. I want a named worker to take that call.

headlineQuote: A ledger can be perfect and still leave a frightened person at the counter.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who reviews restaurant returns.
He has **typical pay**, four months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby firms.
He has **never used AI** and prefers traceable ledgers and colleague-led learning.
He uses the **staff association** to seek error accountability, notice, and severance before any cut.
The **2028** shock alarms him; longer warnings support assigned client practice and new monthly reserves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his review wage before paid client service work appears.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, severance, assigned paid client cases, and signed mortgage-covering job terms.
